newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Kia woes rock S.Korea's stock, currency markets.
newsitem.headline: Kia woes rock S.Korea's stock, currency markets.

text.p: A financial crisis at South Korea's Kia Group sparked concerns of a knock-on impact on banks and other debt-ridden companies that rocked the stock market and battered the local currency on Wednesday.

Kia announced a drastic plan to slim down a day after a consortium of banks and financial institutions stepped in to rescue the nation's eighth-largest business conglomerate and head off a chain reaction of bankruptcies.
But analysts said the moves were little more than a bandage, and Kia was likely to be broken up and sold off, with its car-making flagship company possibly going to the Samsung Group.

Investors rushed to offload shares in Kia's six listed affiliates, sending all six plunging to their limit lows, reflecting fears over the future of the group that has been given an initial two-month reprieve by creditors.
The composite stock index ended 2.03 percent or 15.33 points lower at 739.72.
"Banks took the most severe beating today because of the sheer size of their loans to Kia," said Yoo Bong-keun, a broker at LG Securities. The banking sub-index plunged 5.83 percent.

Dealers said the Bank of Korea intervened five times in the interbank foreign exchange market as investors dumped the local currency on jitters over Kia. The central bank repeatedly sold dollars to prevent the won from sliding.
But the won still ended lower at 893.50 after opening at 892.20. It closed on Tuesday at 891.90.
"Kia's problems potentially could do a lot of damage," said Graham Courtney, director of Asian Economics at SBC Warburg in Tokyo.

"It will make the banks even more loath to lend money, ratcheting up the pressure on companies a couple of notches," he said. "In the short term this will make a lot of smaller companies go bankrupt."
An export downturn and slumping sales at home have hobbled the ability of highly-leveraged conglomerates to service their debt after years of often reckless expansion.
Kia is no exception, having invested heavily in car production and steel-making. Its flagship Kia Motors -- formerly the group's cash cow -- as well as Asia Motors and Kia Steel have been worst hit.
On Wednesday, the group announced it planned to shed half of its 28 domestic affiliates, sell off assets of 1.9 trillion won and cut its work force by 4,300 to 56,000.
But analysts said, at best, the moves would keep the group afloat until after December presidential elections. A big corporate collapse before the vote would be politically unacceptable.
"There is no way to rescue Kia," said Lee Jung-ja, head of research at HSBC James Capel.
"The problem with selling off Kia Steel or Asia Motors is that there is already oversupply in those industries."

To prevent a credit squeeze, the finance ministry said it would pump money into the economy as required. "We will supply money flexibly lest Kia's troubles cause concerns within the financial markets," a ministry statement said.
The central bank supplied one trillion won through repurchase agreements on Tuesday and an additional 500 billion won on Wednesday.
Kia was the third conglomerate, or chaebol, to be rescued by a consortium of banks and financial institutions since April.
Its intervention ensures that Kia's credit lines will remain open and all its loans are rolled over while a more permanent solution is worked out.

The Kia Group had debts of 9.54 trillion won ($10.7 billion) at the end of May, according to the Korea Federation of Banks. Its assets were estimated at 14.6 trillion won by the Korea First Bank, a major creditor.
